name: Light Alice Blue
lede: Light Alice Blue is a pale, slightly greyed blue reached by the word "light" plus [[alice-blue|Alice Blue]], recorded in Ridgway's 1912 color standards and filed again in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955.

sections.title: A modifier on Alice Blue
sections.body:
Our graph builds this name by grammar, not by a new story: "light" plus the parent color [[alice-blue|Alice Blue]], itself named for Alice Roosevelt and recorded by 1902, the date Maerz and Paul give [1][3]. This particular pale swatch is Ridgway's own plate XXXIV, hue 45″, tone d, a scan of an aged printed plate that is only approximate on screen [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 separately filed the name Light Alice Blue itself under block 181, light blue [1]. The parent's screen swatch is a different thing: today's web Alice Blue is a near-white, while Ridgway's chip was a real pale blue [1].

In the color graph, its nearest named neighbor is [[ethereal-blue|Ethereal Blue]], 3.0 units away, with [[russian-blue|Russian Blue]] close behind at 3.5 and [[light-columbia-blue|Light Columbia Blue]] at 4.8 [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this pale blue-grey in 403 of 23,781 paintings, 1.69 percent, as photographed, with the within-painting lens finding it in 263, more common than 73 percent of our named colors [2]. It most often plays a light tone inside a painting, in 52 percent of its matches, and peaks in the 1900s, 30 of the 1,674 paintings we have from that century, 1.4 times the expected rate [2]. Alfred Sisley is its most devoted painter, with 8 of 50 of his works on file carrying it, more than seven times the baseline for the museums that hold them [2]. The earliest dated match runs to 1315, nearly six centuries before Ridgway's 1912 record of the name; that floor is a look-alike hue in an aged, varnished photograph, not evidence that the pigment or the name existed that early [2].
